units.translation: where ἀχεῖν [to sound] is more probable, which the copyists also in Sophocles and Euripides in many places changed into that other verb ἰαχεῖν [to cry aloud], and likewise wrote ἰαχά [a cry] for ἀχά [a sound], about which Elmsley has spoken on Eur. Heracl. 752 and I in Thes. vol. 4 p. 230. But the Doric form of the word ἀχεῖν [to sound] seems to have been admitted not only in the lyric parts of tragedies, but also in anapaests, whence it came about that Aristophanes too in anapaests imitating the language of the tragedians, Vesp. 1489 οἷον μυκτήρ μυκᾶται καὶ | σφόνδυλος ἀχεῖ [as the nostril bellows and the vertebra sounds], although all the other verses are written in Attic, nevertheless preferred to write ἀχεῖ [it sounds] rather than ἠχεῖ [it sounds]. Furthermore in Eurip. Alc. 918 πολυάχητος δ᾽ εἵπετο κῶμος | τήν τε θανοῦσαν κἄμ᾽ ὀλβίζων [and a much-sounding revel followed, blessing the dead woman and me], not πολυήχητος [much-sounding] is read. Therefore Elmsley erred when in the verse of Aeschylus he preferred to write ἠχεῖν [to sound] rather than ἀχεῖν [to sound], which I have restored. The trisyllabic form which had a long middle syllable where needed, the tragedians said ἰακχεῖν [to cry iacche] and ἰακχὴ [the cry iacche], which the copyists are accustomed to write ἰαχή [a cry] and ἰαχεῖν [to cry aloud], about which I have spoken under the word ἰακχή [the cry iacche].
to raise the ill-sounding hymn of the Fury, and to chant the hateful paean to Hades
as the nostril bellows and the vertebra sounds
and a much-sounding revel followed, blessing the dead woman and me
this light is not without ancestry from the Idaean fire
